post.caption: 🛢️ A war that started in the Gulf in February has shut the world's busiest oil route — and it's landing at Ghana's fuel pumps. Here's the timeline, and why you feel it. 🇬🇭
post.body: The US–Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carries about a fifth of the world's oil, and shipping there has collapsed from ~100 vessels a day to under 10. Ghana imports ~70% of its fuel in dollars — so petrol climbed to about GH¢13.30 a litre and inflation rose for the first time in 16 months.

chapters.say: A war that began in the Gulf in February has now closed the world's key oil route and reached all the way to Ghana's fuel pumps.
The United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on the twenty eighth of February, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and igniting a regional war.
The fighting shut the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel that carries about one fifth of the world's oil, with almost no alternative route.
A ceasefire agreed in April collapsed in July after Iran attacked commercial ships, and United States bombing then ran for thirteen straight nights.
Fewer than ten ships now pass through Hormuz each day, down from about one hundred, and oil has swung back near one hundred dollars a barrel.
Ghana imports about seventy percent of its fuel, so petrol climbed near thirteen cedis a litre and inflation rose for the first time in sixteen months.
By late July the United States had paused its strikes, but with talks stalled, whether Ghana's prices ease depends on a fragile calm holding.
